Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Nay, I swear by this city, (1) and you are a freeman of this city﴾ [Al-Balad 1, 2].

I have a brief digression on what was covered in the previous lesson, concerning the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿﴿So on that Day none will punish as He punishes, and none will bind as He binds﴾ ﴾ [Al-Fajr 25, 26]. I recited it in this way and explained it according to this reading, because there are two readings of the two verses mentioned. The first reading, which is in the Mushaf: ﴿So on that Day none will punish as He punishes (25) and none will bind as He binds﴾, meaning: no one punishes the punishment of Allah, rather the punishment of Allah is more severe, and no one binds the binding of Allah, rather His binding is more severe.

As for the reading ﴿﴿None punishes His punishment anyone﴾﴾, meaning: no one punishes the punishment of this man, and no one binds the binding of this man. This is the reading upon which we recited the verse and explained it, and for this reason the notice was given.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Nay, I swear by this city﴾ [Al-Balad 1]. The ﴿Nay﴾ here is for opening the speech, for introducing the statement and for emphasis; it is not a negation, because the intended meaning is affirming the oath. That is: I swear by this city. But this ﴿Nay﴾ comes here for alerting and emphasis.

And ﴿I swear﴾: qasam (oath) is affirming a matter by mentioning something held in great esteem in a specific manner. So every thing sworn by must necessarily be held in esteem by the one swearing, though it may not be esteemed in itself. For example, those who swear by al-Lat and al-'Uzza, these are esteemed by them, but in reality they are neither great nor esteemed. Therefore, hilf (swearing), qasam, or yamin (oath) — the meaning is one — is affirming a matter by what? By mentioning something esteemed. In whose view? In the view of the one swearing, in a specific attribute.

The letters of qasam are: the ba', the waw, and the ta'. And what is in this noble verse here: ﴿I swear by this city﴾, which letter? The ba'.

﴿By this city﴾: the city here is Makkah, and Allah swore by it for its nobility and greatness. It is the most sacred of the lands of the earth, and the dearest of the lands of the earth to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who is the master of mankind, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, was sent from it. Thus this secure city is worthy of being sworn by. But we do not swear by it, because it is a creation, and we do not have the right to swear by a creation; as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears by other than Allah has disbelieved," or: "has associated partners [with Allah]" [[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (1535) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. As for Allah the Mighty and Majestic, He swears by whatever He wills, and for this reason He swore here by Makkah: ﴿Nay, I swear by this city﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 90 (al-Balad), verse 2:**

﴿And you, [O Muhammad], are a resident of this city.﴾ [al-Balad: 2].

It has been said: the meaning is, "I swear by this city while you are residing in it," because the residence of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Makkah increases it in nobility beyond its own nobility.

It has also been said: the meaning is, "And you make this city lawful (permissible for yourself)," so that Allah's oath by Makkah is taken while it was made lawful for the Messenger (ﷺ), and that was on the Day of the Conquest. For Makkah on the Day of the Conquest was made lawful for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and it was not made lawful for anyone before him, nor will it be made lawful for anyone after him. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Its sanctity has returned today as it was sanctified yesterday."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1832) and Muslim (1354 / 446), from the hadith of Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Thus Allah's oath by this city is restricted to the case in which it was lawful for the Messenger. And when was that? On the Day of the Conquest. For on that day it increases in nobility beyond its own nobility, in that it was purified from the idols, the polytheists were defeated, and their lands were conquered by force. This city, which had been a land of disbelief, became a land of faith; and which had been a land of polytheism, became a land of monotheism; and which had been a land of obstinacy, became a land of Islam. So the most noble state of Makkah was at the Conquest. Therefore, in His saying ﴿And you are a resident of this city﴾ there are two meanings, which I hope are on your mind.

"I swear by this city (1), and you are a resident of this city (2), and by the begetter and what he begot (3)."

[Al-Balad: 1-3] That is: "And I swear by the begetter and what he begot." So who is meant by the begetter, and who is meant by what he begot?

It has been said: the begetter is Adam, and what he begot is the children of Adam. On this view, "ma" (what) is in the sense of "man" (who), meaning "and the begetter and whoever he begot," because "man" is used for rational beings and "ma" for non-rational beings.

It has also been said: what is meant by the begetter and what he begot is every begetter and what he begets: man, animals, and everything else, because both the begetter and the begotten are among the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Consider, for example, how this child comes forth alive, well-formed, hearing and seeing, from a drop of fluid, from water! This is evidence of the perfect power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This well-formed child emerges from a drop; ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop [of semen], and then he is an open adversary?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 77]. Likewise, insects and others emerge weak and frail, then grow to whatever extent Allah the Exalted wills. ﴿And by the begetter and what he begot﴾. So the correct view is that this is general, encompassing every begetter and every begotten.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 90, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, We created man in toil.﴾ [al-Balad: 4] The lam here is the lam of the response to the oath, to add emphasis to the sentence, and (qad) also adds emphasis, so the sentence ﴿Indeed, We created man﴾ is emphasized by three emphatics: the oath, the second, the lam, and the third, (qad).

﴿Indeed, We created man in toil.﴾ ﴿Al-insan (man)﴾ is a generic noun that includes every one of the children of Adam.

﴿In toil (kabad)﴾ has two meanings:

The first meaning: in uprightness. That is, he was created in the most complete form of creation, upright, walking on his two feet, raising his head, with a balanced body, whereas the animals are the opposite: the head is level with the rear. Is that not so? As for the children of Adam, no; the head is raised above the body. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We created man in the best of stature.﴾ [al-Tin: 4]

It has also been said that the intended meaning of kabad is struggling with things and bearing their hardships, and that man endures hardship in worldly affairs: in seeking provision, in cultivating the land, and in other things. He also endures a greater hardship with himself, striving against it to obey Allah and to avoid the disobedience of Allah. This is the struggle that is harder than the hardship of seeking provision, especially when a person is tested with a deviant environment and becomes a stranger among them, for he will find hardship both in struggling with his own self and in dealing with people.

If someone says: Could the verse not include both meanings?

The answer: Yes. This is how it should be when you find in the Mighty Book a verse that may bear two meanings with no contradiction between them; then carry it on both meanings, because the Qur'an is more comprehensive and broader. If there is a contradiction between them, then consider which is preponderant. For example, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three quru'* (periods)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]. ﴿Quru'* ﴾ is the plural of qar' (with a fatha on the qaf). So what is the qar'? It has been said: it is menstruation. And it has been said: it is purity (tuhr). Here it is not possible to carry the verse on both meanings together, why? Because of the contradiction. Rather, seek the preponderant opinion of one of the two views and adopt it.

So here we say: ﴿Indeed, We created man in toil﴾ may validly include both meanings; that is, in a good stature and uprightness, and ﴿in toil﴾ in struggling with the hardships of affairs.

Let us limit ourselves to this measure of the clear signs of Allah so that we may be free for the questions, and we ask Allah, glorified and exalted, to make us all among those who recite His Book with its due recitation, and to bestow upon us mercy from Him, for He is the Bestower.

(...) This is the meeting held with the brothers each week, and this is the seventieth meeting, which takes place in Rabi' al-Awwal of the year one thousand four hundred and fifteen. It is our custom to first speak about the tafsir of verses we were with from Surah al-Naba' until we reached the beginning of Surah al-Balad, in His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We created man in toil (4). Does he think that no one will ever have power over him? (5) He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance." (6) Does he think that no one has seen him?﴾ [al-Balad: 4–7]. We explained that His saying, ﴿Indeed, We created man in toil﴾, has two meanings among the scholars:

The first meaning: kabad means perfection and elevation in creation, intellect, and other things.

The second meaning: in struggling with the hardships of worldly and otherworldly affairs.

The rule in interpreting the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, O our brothers, is that when a verse may bear two meanings and there is no contradiction between them, it is carried on both meanings together, because that is broader in interpretation and knowledge.

Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, says: ﴿Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?﴾ [Al-Balad 5]. The meaning is that man, in himself and in his strength, thinks that no one will ever have power over him, because he is in the prime of his youth, his strength, his pride and his arrogance. So he says: "No one has power over me; I do whatever I wish." Among the same meaning is the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right and said, "Who is greater than us in strength?"﴾ Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is greater than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15].

So man, in the state of his health and the prime of his youth, thinks that no one has power over him. This is undoubtedly the case for the disbeliever, even regarding the Lord, Exalted and Majestic; he thinks that He has no power over him. As for the believer, he knows that Allah is capable over him and that He is Able over everything, so he fears Allah.

Translation:

﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ [Al-Balad: 6] The human being also says, in a state of his wealth and the expansion of provision for him: ﴿"I have squandered wealth in abundance"﴾. That is: wealth in great quantity, spent on his desires and on his pleasures.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Does he think that no one sees him?﴾ [Al-Balad 7] Does this one think that no one sees him in his squandering of wealth and spending it on what does not benefit? And all of this is a warning to man: that he should not act arrogantly and should not be haughty because of his physical strength or the abundance of his wealth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 90, verse 8–10:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes? And a tongue and two lips? And guide him to the two highways?﴾ [Al-Balad 8–10]. These are three of the greatest blessings upon man.

﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?﴾ [Al-Balad 8] meaning, by which he sees and perceives. These two eyes convey to the heart what a person looks at. If he looks at a forbidden thing, he is sinful; if he looks in a way that brings him closer to Allah, he is a gainer; and if he looks at what is permissible for him, he is neither praised nor blamed, so long as this looking does not lead to a legally prohibited matter, in which case he becomes sinful through that look.

﴿And a tongue and two lips﴾ [Al-Balad 9]: a tongue with which he speaks, and two lips with which he controls speech. This is one of Allah's great blessings, for by this tongue and these two lips he is able to express what is in himself. Without this, he could not do so. If he did not speak, how could he convey what is in his heart? How could he make people aware of what is within him? Except by a gesture that is tiring: he tires himself, the one gesturing, and the one to whom the gesture is made tires as well. But it is among Allah's blessings that He made for him a speaking tongue and two lips with which he controls speech. This is a blessing of Allah, and it is also one of the wonders of His power. From where does speech come? From air that comes from the lungs and exits from specific points of articulation. If it passes over one thing it becomes one letter, and if it passes over another thing it becomes a different letter, though it is one air from one exit. It passes through tiny fibers in the throat, in the lips, and in the gums, and these fibers form the letters. So you find, for example, that the *bā'* (ب) and the *shīn* (ش) are all from air propelled from the lungs, yet they differ according to what it passes over in this mouth and the known points of articulation of the letters. This is part of the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He said: ﴿And guided him to the two highways﴾ [Al-Balad 10]. ﴿Guided him﴾ means: We made clear to him the path of good and the path of evil. This is one opinion.

The second opinion: ﴿guided him to the two highways﴾ means We showed him what sustains him, which is the two breasts, for they are two highways because of their elevation above the chest. Allah guided him while he was an infant who knows nothing: from the moment he comes out and his mother places him, he seeks the breast. Who taught him? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus Allah the Mighty and Majestic makes clear His favour upon this human being: from the moment he comes out, he is guided to the two highways.

In the womb of his mother, he is nourished through the umbilical cord, because he cannot be nourished by any other means. Had he been nourished through the mouth, he would need urine and feces. And how could that be? Rather, it is through the umbilical cord: blood comes to him from his mother's blood and spreads through his veins until he lives, until Allah the Exalted permits his coming out.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [Al-Balad 11] and (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 90, verse 11–13:

We begin this session by completing the discussion of Surah al-Balad, where we stopped at the words of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿But he has not attempted the ascent (11) And what can make you know what the ascent is? (12) It is the freeing of a neck (13)﴾ to the end of the surah.

﴿But he has not attempted﴾ means: the human being who used to say, "I have squandered abundant wealth." ﴿But he has not attempted the ascent﴾ means: why did he not attempt the ascent? Iqtiham (attempting, plunging into) is crossing over something with hardship; crossing over something with hardship is called iqtiham. And the 'aqabah (steep path, ascent) is the path up a rugged mountain. There is no doubt that attempting this ascent is difficult and burdensome for the souls, and no one undertakes it except one who has a sincere intention to cross this ascent.

﴿And what can make you know what the ascent is?﴾ This interrogation is also for arousing interest and magnifying the matter; meaning: what has informed you of the nature of this ascent about which Allah said: ﴿But he has not attempted the ascent﴾?

Allah explained it by His saying: ﴿It is the freeing of a neck (13) Or feeding on a day of severe hunger (14) An orphan of near relationship (15) Or a needy man in misery (16) Then being among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad 13–17] to the end of it.

As for His saying: ﴿the freeing of a neck﴾ [al-Balad 13], it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the implied meaning is: it is the freeing of a neck. The freeing of a neck has two meanings:

The first meaning: freeing it from bondage, such that a person frees enslaved people, whether they are under his ownership, so he frees them, or they are under the ownership of another, so he buys them and frees them. This is one type.

The second type: freeing a neck from captivity. Indeed, ransoming a captive is among the best deeds in the sight of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The captive may not be released by the enemy except for a large financial ransom, and this ransom may be exorbitant and great, which none will undertake except one who has faith in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He will replace what he spent and reward him for what he gave in charity.

So the freeing of a neck has two meanings:

The first meaning: freeing the neck from bondage, by liberating it; if it is under his ownership, then in his ownership, and otherwise he buys it and liberates it.

And the second: freeing the neck from captivity.

Allah says: ﴿Or feeding on a day of severe hunger﴾ [Al-Balad 14]. ﴿Or﴾ here is for variety; meaning: or else, feeding on a day of severe hunger, i.e., a day of intense famine. This is because people may be struck by severe famine either due to a scarcity of produce from fruits and crops, or due to illnesses in their bodies, where a person eats and yet is not satisfied. This has indeed occurred, as we have heard: it has happened in the Najdi lands and perhaps elsewhere too, that people eat and are not satisfied; one person eats the meal of ten and is still not satisfied, and people die of hunger in the markets, collapsing in the markets from hunger. These are among the times of hunger (masghaba).

Or (it may be due to) a scarcity of harvest, such that the trees do not bear fruit and the crops do not grow, so the produce becomes scarce and famine (masghaba) occurs, and people die of hunger, and perhaps they migrate away from their lands.

﴿Orphan of near relationship﴾ [Al-Balad: 15, 16]. ﴿An orphan﴾: the orphan is one whose father has died before he reaches maturity, whether male or female. If he reaches maturity, he is no longer an orphan, because he has come of age and become independent. The same applies if his mother dies: he does not thereby become an orphan. This differs from what some of the common people believe, that an orphan is one whose mother has died. This is not correct. The orphan is one whose father has died, because when his father dies, he has no earner among the creatures to earn for him.

His words, ﴿of near relationship﴾, mean one who is related to the person, because when he is an orphan he has a share of honour and charity, and when he is a relative his share of that increases, because he becomes someone whose ties must be upheld. So whoever combines these two qualities, orphanhood and kinship, then providing food for him is among the "breaking through the steep path" (iqtiham al-'aqabah, the difficult ascent of the Qur'an, Al-Balad 90:11) when this happens on a day of hunger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 90, verse 16:

﴿Or a needy person in distress﴾ [al-Balad: 16]. Meaning: or feeding, on a day of hunger, a needy person in distress.

Al-miskin (the needy person, one who lacks sustenance): he is the one who does not find his own sustenance or the sustenance of his dependents. Al-matraba (the state of being in the dust, i.e., destitution): it refers to the place of dust. The meaning is that he is a needy person who has nothing in his hands except dust. It is well known that when it is said of a man, "He has nothing but dust," the meaning is that he is extremely poor: he has no food, he has no clothing, he has no wealth. So he is a needy person in the dust (miskin dhu matraba).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 90, verse 17:

﴿Then he became one of those who believed and enjoined one another to patience and enjoined one another to compassion.﴾ [Al-Balad: 17].

﴿Then he became﴾ means: then, after that, he is not one who does good to orphans and the needy, but rather he is one who has faith in Allah.

﴿Then he became one of those who believed and enjoined one another to patience and enjoined one another to compassion.﴾ Those who believed in what? They believed in everything that must be believed in. The Messenger (ﷺ) explained what must be believed in, when Jibril asked him about faith (iman), and he said: "Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree (qadar), its good and its evil."[[Narrated by Muslim (8), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (177), with this wording, from the hadith of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

And His saying: ﴿and enjoined one another to patience﴾ means: they urged one another to be patient. Patience is of three kinds: patience in obeying Allah, patience in refraining from disobeying Allah, and patience in the face of Allah's painful decrees. So they are patient and enjoin one another to patience. And which of these kinds is best? The best is patience in obeying Allah, then patience in refraining from disobeying Allah, then patience in the face of Allah's painful decrees. These three kinds have been combined in the messengers, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon them, and in their followers.

Behold the Messenger (ﷺ) was patient in obeying Allah: he strove in the way of Allah, called to Allah, was harmed, and was attacked and beaten, to the point that the polytheists intended to kill him, yet he remained patient, seeking his reward from Allah.

He was also patient in refraining from disobeying Allah: he could never betray anyone, nor lie to anyone, nor deceive anyone, and he was also mindful of Allah, Exalted is He, to the extent of his ability.

Likewise, he was patient in obeying Allah: how much was he harmed for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because of his obedience to Him? Did not the Quraysh harm him to the point that, when they saw him prostrating beneath the Ka'bah, they ordered someone to bring the entrails of a she-camel and place them on his back while he was prostrating, peace and blessings be upon him, and he remained patient in all of that.

Yusuf (peace be upon him) was patient in the face of Allah's decrees: he was thrown into the well, into the depths of the pit, and was harmed for the sake of Allah by imprisonment, yet he was patient, seeking his reward, did not complain, and did not reject what befell him.

And His saying: ﴿and enjoined one another to compassion﴾ means: they urged one another to show mercy to others. Compassion is the mercy of a person toward creatures; it exists toward animals and toward rational beings. He shows mercy to his fathers and mothers, his sons and daughters, his brothers and sisters, his paternal uncles and aunts, and so on; he likewise shows mercy to all people, and he also shows mercy to dumb animals, so he shows mercy to his she-camel, his horse, his donkey, his cow, his sheep, and others. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Show mercy to those on the earth, and He who is in heaven will show mercy to you."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (1924) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both).]]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 90, verse 18:

﴿Those are the companions of the right hand (ashab al-maymanah)﴾ [al-Balad: 18]. ﴿Those﴾ means: those who are described by these attributes. ﴿The companions of the right hand﴾ means: the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), who will be given their books on the Day of Resurrection in their right hands; ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will be called to a light account, and will return to his family joyful﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 7-9].

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And those who disbelieved in Our signs—they are the companions of the left hand﴾ [Al-Balad 19].

When He mentioned the believers, He mentioned the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved in Our signs﴾, meaning: those who denied them (jahadu biha). ﴿They are the companions of the left hand (ashab al-mash'ama)﴾. The pronoun here (huwa) comes for emphasis (li-l-tawkid). Had it been said outside the Qur'an, "And those who disbelieved in Our signs, the companions of the left hand," it would have been correct; but this is from the category of emphasis (tawkid). And ﴿al-mash'ama﴾ means the left side (al-shimal) or misfortune (al-shu'm).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 90, verse 20:

﴿Upon them will be fire, sealed shut.﴾ [Al-Balad: 20] That is: upon them is a fire that is closed shut, from which—we seek refuge in Allah—they will not come out, nor will they be able to.

We ask Allah to make us and you among those who believe and do righteous deeds, and who enjoin one another to patience and enjoin one another to mercy.
